html:
The Turkish Civil Code of 1926 was a new law of family, property and contracts for the young Republic of Turkey. It was a near translation of the Swiss Civil Code, and it replaced Islamic law in private life.

Under the Ottoman Empire, marriage, divorce and inheritance had followed sharia as applied by religious courts, with separate rules for Christian and Jewish communities. Mustafa Kemal's government wanted one secular law for all citizens.

  • It banned polygamy and required civil marriage.
  • Divorce went through the courts, on equal grounds for husband and wife.
  • Daughters and sons inherited equal shares.
  • Women could act as witnesses on an equal footing.

Change in villages was slow, and religious marriages went on unofficially. But the code was one of the deepest of the Kemalist reforms, alongside the new alphabet. Its story is also told as Turkey adopts the Swiss Civil Code. A revised code came into force in 2002.
